42933915|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|0e9e19.relation_evidence: The OCEAN-Mitral registry is a prospective, non-randomised registry of M-TEER patients with severe MR of mixed aetiology, so it differs in design and population from COAPT (2023) and RESHAPE-HF2 (2024), which were randomised trials in secondary MR with heart failure and reported hospitalisation and death endpoints against medical therapy alone. COAPT (2023) and RESHAPE-HF2 (2024) did not stratify outcomes by periprocedural pulmonary pressure change, so the registry's grouping into normalized, new-onset and residual PH adds a post-procedural haemodynamic dimension to the outcome picture rather than confirming or contradicting them. The registry's 2-year composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation is similar in kind to the RESHAPE-HF2 (2024) primary endpoint, but the registry has no medical-therapy comparator. No consensus paper in the list addresses PH dynamics after M-TEER.
42933915|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|0e9e19.relation_guidelines: ESC/EACTS 2025 lists TEER for severe ventricular SMR (Class I, Level A) in symptomatic patients with LVEF <50% and persistent severe MR despite optimized GDMT and CRT, fulfilling specific clinical and echocardiographic criteria. In the ESC 2025 primary MR algorithm, SPAP at rest >50 mmHg appears as one of the features for TEER consideration. ESC Heart Failure Guidelines (2021) set systolic pulmonary pressure <70 mmHg among the criteria for TEER aimed at reducing HF hospitalisation (Class IIa, Level B). These documents use pre-procedural pulmonary pressure as a selection criterion, whereas the registry examines the change in PH status after the procedure and its association with 2-year outcomes, which the quoted guideline text does not address.
42933915|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|0e9e19.tension: The guidelines use pre-procedural systolic pulmonary pressure thresholds for patient selection, while the registry reports prognostic associations of post-procedural PH status (residual or new-onset PH) that the guideline text does not address.

42910974|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|14b9e7.relation_evidence: The listed trials (SURTAVI 2022, UK TAVI 2022, DEDICATE-DZHK6 2024) compare TAVI with surgical aortic valve replacement in intermediate- or low-to-intermediate-risk patients and do not address coronary revascularisation versus conservative management. The new meta-analysis therefore examines a different question (PCI strategy in patients already referred for TAVI, with MACE as primary endpoint) and cannot be directly compared with their endpoints of death or stroke. 42910974|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|14b9e7.relation_guidelines: ESC 2025 lists as a new recommendation that PCI should be considered in patients with a primary indication for TAVI and ≥90% coronary stenosis in segments with a reference diameter ≥2.5 mm (class IIa, level B). The new meta-analysis pools trials of routine PCI versus conservative treatment and reports lower MACE and unplanned revascularisation with PCI, alongside more major bleeding. ESC 2025 also lists omission of invasive coronary angiography as a consideration (IIa, B) when planning CT angiography rules out significant CAD, but this does not bear directly on the revascularisation comparison.
42910974|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|14b9e7.tension: The meta-analysis reports benefit of routine PCI and of physiology-guided PCI, whereas the ESC 2025 recommendation is tied to an angiographic stenosis threshold (≥90%) and does not address physiology-guided revascularisation or routine PCI regardless of stenosis severity.

42948592|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|05d794.relation_evidence: The OCEAN-TAVI registry is an observational, non-randomised analysis of contemporary valves (SAPIEN 3 Ultra RESILIA, Evolut FX, Navitor) with in-hospital stroke as the endpoint. The randomised trials differ in design, endpoint and valve generation. SURTAVI (2022) used an earlier-generation self-expanding platform and reported a 5-year composite of death or disabling stroke of 31.3% after TAVR versus 30.8% after surgery. DEDICATE-DZHK6 (2024) reported 1-year stroke of 2.9% after TAVI versus 4.7% after surgery with freely chosen valve systems. UK TAVI (2022) described numerically more strokes after TAVI without statistical certainty, and its mixed use of CE-marked valves limited device-specific conclusions. The registry's comparison of stroke rates between individual contemporary valve platforms, and its 1-year survival after in-hospital stroke, are not addressed in these trials, so the findings extend rather than confirm or contradict them.
42948592|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|05d794.relation_guidelines: ESC 2025 states that SAVR or TAVI are recommended (Class I, level B) for all remaining candidates for an aortic bioprosthetic valve according to Heart Team assessment. It also states that non-transfemoral TAVI should be considered (Class IIa, level B) in patients unsuitable for surgery and transfemoral access. The registry identified non-transfemoral access and prior stroke as independent associates of in-hospital stroke, which relates to the access-route statement, but ESC 2025 gives no stroke-risk comparison between access routes or between valve platforms. Its antithrombotic section after bioprosthetic valve implantation refers to GALILEO and the use of OAC or aspirin, whereas the registry does not analyse antithrombotic regimens.
42948592|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|05d794.tension: The registry reports differences in in-hospital stroke and disabling stroke between individual contemporary valve platforms, a level of device-specific distinction that the ESC 2025 recommendations on TAVI do not address.

42933524|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|b8de81.relation_evidence: This narrative review of randomized trials, meta-analyses and propensity-matched registries emphasises time-dependent treatment effects and durability uncertainty. The randomized low-risk trials listed show a mixed picture. PARTNER 3 (2025) reported similar composite outcomes at 7 years, with numerically higher cumulative death after TAVR than after surgery, and Evolut Low Risk (2025) reported similar 5-year death or disabling stroke. NOTION-2 (3-year, 2025) showed a numerically higher composite event rate after TAVR, particularly in the bicuspid subgroup, and NOTION (10-year, 2024) showed identical combined endpoints in an older cohort. The review's concern about attenuation of early TAVI non-inferiority and about durability and reintervention in younger patients is consistent with the longer-term caveats in these trials. Its reliance on propensity-matched registry signals of late mortality is a different design from the randomized data, which did not show a significant difference.
42933524|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|b8de81.relation_guidelines: ESC 2025: TAVI is recommended (Class I, Level A) in patients ≥70 years with tricuspid aortic valve stenosis if the anatomy is suitable, and SAVR is recommended (Class I, Level B) in patients <70 years if surgical risk is low. ESC 2025 also recommends (Class I, Level C) that the mode of intervention be based on Heart Team assessment of individual clinical, anatomical and procedural characteristics, incorporating lifetime management considerations and estimated life expectancy. The review's framework of Heart Team-based, individualized decisions weighted by life expectancy and lifetime management corresponds to this wording. Its positioning of SAVR as a central reference strategy in patients with long expected survival is presented as an application of these recommendations.
42933524|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|b8de81.tension: The review's emphasis on SAVR as a reference strategy in patients with long life expectancy, including those aged 70 years or older, sits alongside the age-based Class I recommendation for TAVI in ≥70-year-olds with suitable anatomy in ESC 2025, a threshold that does not itself distinguish by individual life expectancy.

The ESC statement already includes lifetime management considerations and estimated life expectancy, so the tension is modest.

42949674|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|8f54f9.relation_guidelines: ESC/EACTS 2025 (valvular heart disease) notes that in non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome it may be particularly challenging to determine the leading cause of elevated troponin, because troponin elevation is also frequently seen in decompensated valvular heart disease. For this setting, ESC/EACTS 2025 states that the treatment strategy is determined by the Heart Team, taking into account symptoms and coronary, valve and access anatomy. The new review addresses the same difficulty of attributing troponin elevation, but across a broader set of conditions (chronic kidney disease, heart failure, sepsis, tachyarrhythmias, pulmonary embolism, takotsubo syndrome) and through the Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction. It also describes assay-specific and sex-specific thresholds and serial-testing algorithms, which the valvular guideline text does not discuss.
42949674|en|2.1|claude-sonnet-5-5|8f54f9.tension: The review treats troponin classification (injury versus necrosis versus infarction, including chronic myocardial injury) as a general interpretive problem across many diseases, whereas the ESC/EACTS 2025 statement on troponin is limited to non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome in patients with valvular heart disease.
